title: Arc-Sprayed Aluminium Coating on the Nigeria LNG Train 7 Project: Application Quality, Short-Term Immersion Corrosion and the Limits of Service-Life Extrapolation
content: Thermally sprayed aluminium (TSA) is being adopted to reduce maintenance painting on liquefied natural gas (LNG) plants, yet no performance data exist for the Niger Delta. This study documents the arc-sprayed TSA applied on the Nigeria LNG Train 7 project (Bonny Island, about 50,000 m2) and evaluates its short-term corrosion behaviour. Surface preparation and coating quality were verified against ISO and SSPC requirements: Sa 2½ cleanliness, anchor profile 89 ± 11 µm, soluble salt 0.90 ± 0.22 µg cm−2, dust level 1, dry film thickness 447 ± 89 µm and pull-off adhesion 20.5 ± 2.1 MPa (n = 10); all 180° bend tests passed. Companion coupons were immersed in 5 wt% NaCl for 7-28 days in three beeswax-masked configurations that isolated bare steel, the TSA coating and the coupled steel/TSA system, and corrosion rates were derived from mass loss. After 28 days the apparent corrosion rate of TSA was 0.49 mm y−1, against 1.48 mm y−1 for bare steel; cumulative mass loss of both materials increased linearly with time (R2 > 0.99), and TSA was consumed about three times more slowly than steel. Coupled specimens showed rapid sacrificial consumption of the aluminium where the coating-to-steel area ratio was small. Because short-term rates in NaCl reflect activation of a fresh, porous coating and lack the protective films that form in natural seawater, they cannot be extrapolated linearly to service life; doing so would predict coating exhaustion within a year, contrary to multi-decade field evidence. A site exposure programme at Bonny is proposed.
